Items.Name: Artifact
Items.Doc:
One thing a build produces: a `.lyrbc` compiled from an entry file.

Returned by `addExecutable`, and configured after the fact — the compile itself happens once
`build` has returned, so an option set on the next line still applies.

Items.Name: addExecutable
Items.Signature: pub fn addExecutable(entry: string, output: string): Artifact
Items.Doc:
Declares a program to compile: `entry` is its main file, `output` the `.lyrbc` to write.

Both are relative to the directory holding `build.lyr`. The module root and the native roots
come from `lyric.json`; this does not repeat them.

Nothing is compiled while `build` runs. The artifacts are collected and built afterwards, so
work the script does in between — writing a generated source file, for instance — is finished
before any of them is read.

Items.Name: Indexable
Items.Doc:
What can be read and written with `[i]`.

The same model as `Iterator<T>` for `for-in`: the compiler knows one built-in form — the array —
and binds everything else to an interface from the standard library, so there is no special case
per container type.

`get` and `set` are O(1). That is a requirement, not a description: an implementation with O(n)
access must not satisfy this interface, or an index loop would be quadratic without showing it.
`string` has no index operator for the same reason.

Members.Name: get
Members.Doc: The value at `index`.

Members.Name: set
Members.Signature: mut fn set(index: int, value: T): void
Members.Doc: Replaces the value at `index`.

Items.Name: List
Items.Doc:
A growing list; a `T[]` has a fixed length, this does not.

Growing doubles and shrinking halves at a quarter, so `push` is amortized O(1) and a list
oscillating around a boundary does not copy on every step.

Members.Name: data
Members.Doc: The backing slots; optional so a popped slot can actually release its value.

Members.Name: count
Members.Doc: How many slots are filled.

Members.Name: length
Members.Doc: How many values are in it.

Members.Name: empty
Members.Doc: An empty list.

Members.Name: iter
Members.Doc: A fresh cursor on every call, so two loops over the same list do not disturb each other.

Members.Name: isEmpty
Members.Doc: Whether nothing is in it.

Members.Name: capacity
Members.Doc:
How many slots are allocated, empty ones included. For tests and for anyone measuring what
the list costs; `length` is the truth for everything else.

Members.Name: push
Members.Signature: pub mut fn push(value: T): void
Members.Doc: Appends at the end; amortized O(1).

Members.Name: pop
Members.Doc:
Removes and returns the last value, or `null` for an empty list — an ordinary state,
unlike an index out of range.

Members.Name: get
Members.Doc:
The value at `index`. Out of range is a panic, as for an array: a programming error
rather than a state.

Members.Name: set
Members.Signature: pub mut fn set(index: int, value: T): void
Members.Doc: Replaces the value at `index`. Out of range is a panic, as in `get`.

Members.Name: clear
Members.Doc:
Empties the list. Every slot is released — nothing inserted stays alive — but the
backing array is KEPT: a buffer emptied once per frame must not reallocate on every
refill.

Members.Name: first
Members.Doc: The first value, or `null` for an empty list.

Members.Name: last
Members.Doc: The last value, or `null` for an empty list.

Members.Name: insert
Members.Signature: pub mut fn insert(index: int, value: T): void
Members.Doc:
Inserts at `index`, shifting everything from there one to the right. `index == length()`
appends. Out of range is a panic, as in `get`.

Members.Name: removeAt
Members.Signature: pub mut fn removeAt(index: int): T
Members.Doc:
Removes and returns the value at `index`, shifting the rest left. Out of range is a
panic, as in `get`.

Members.Name: reverse
Members.Doc: Reverses in place.

Members.Name: swap
Members.Signature: pub mut fn swap(a: int, b: int): void
Members.Doc: Exchanges two positions. Out of range is a panic, as in `get`.

Members.Name: toArray
Members.Doc: A copy as a real array.

Items.Name: emptyList
Items.Doc: An empty list.

Items.Name: ListIterator
Items.Doc: Walks a list; each loop holds its own cursor.

Members.Name: source
Members.Doc: The list being walked.

Members.Name: index
Members.Doc: The next slot to look at.

Members.Name: next
Members.Doc: The next value, or `null` at the end.

Items.Name: collect
Items.Doc:
Collects an iterator into a `List<T>`.

Here rather than in `std.iter`, because the dependency runs this way: `std.collections` imports
`std.iter`, not the reverse. `std.iter.collectArray` is the variant without that dependency,
and it is quadratic because a `T[]` copies on every append. This one doubles and is linear.

Items.Name: Map
Items.Doc:
A hash map: open addressing, linear probing, load factor 3/4. The key type says how to
hash and how to compare — `[Hashable<K>, Equatable<K>]` — and the iteration order is
UNSPECIFIED.

Members.Name: keys
Members.Doc: The key column; `states` says which slots are real.

Members.Name: values
Members.Doc: The value column, parallel to `keys`.

Members.Name: states
Members.Doc: Per slot: 0 empty, 1 occupied, 2 tombstone.

Members.Name: count
Members.Doc: The occupied slots alone.

Members.Name: used
Members.Doc: Occupied plus tombstones — what the load factor is measured over.

Members.Name: length
Members.Doc: How many values are in it.

Members.Name: isEmpty
Members.Doc: Whether nothing is in it.

Members.Name: empty
Members.Signature: pub static fn empty(): Map<K, V>
Members.Doc: An empty map, with room for the first insertions before a growth.

Members.Name: containsKey
Members.Doc: Whether the key is in the map.

Members.Name: get
Members.Doc: The value for the key, or `null` when the key is absent.

Members.Name: set
Members.Signature: pub mut fn set(key: K, value: V): void
Members.Doc: Inserts, or overwrites the existing entry for an equal key.

Members.Name: getOr
Members.Signature: pub fn getOr(key: K, fallback: V): V
Members.Doc:
The value for the key, or `fallback` when the key is absent — one probe instead of a
`containsKey` before every `get`.

Members.Name: clear
Members.Doc:
Empties the map. The backing arrays are KEPT, as in `List.clear`; the tombstones vanish
with everything else.

Members.Name: remove
Members.Doc: Removes and returns the old value, or `null` when the key was absent.

Items.Name: emptyMap
Items.Signature: pub fn emptyMap<K :: [Hashable<K>, Equatable<K>], V>(): Map<K, V>
Items.Doc: An empty map.

Items.Name: sortList
Items.Doc: Sorts in place by the natural order of the type.

Items.Name: sortListBy
Items.Signature: pub fn sortListBy<T>(xs: List<T>, less: fn(T, T) -> bool): void
Items.Doc:
Sorts in place with a comparison of your own.

`less(a, b)` must return `true` when `a` comes STRICTLY before `b`. A `less` returning `true`
for equal elements destroys stability; a contradictory `less` makes the output arbitrary but
crashes nothing, because the algorithm only compares.

Items.Name: Set
Items.Doc:
A hash set: the same probing as `Map`, without the value column. Iteration order is
UNSPECIFIED. `Iterable`, so `for (v in set)` walks it directly.

Members.Name: items
Members.Doc: The element column; `states` says which slots are real.

Members.Name: states
Members.Doc: Per slot: 0 empty, 1 occupied, 2 tombstone.

Members.Name: count
Members.Doc: The occupied slots alone.

Members.Name: used
Members.Doc: Occupied plus tombstones — what the load factor is measured over.

Members.Name: length
Members.Doc: How many values are in it.

Members.Name: isEmpty
Members.Doc: Whether nothing is in it.

Members.Name: empty
Members.Doc: An empty set.

Members.Name: contains
Members.Doc: Whether the value is in the set.

Members.Name: add
Members.Signature: pub mut fn add(value: T): bool
Members.Doc:
Adds and returns `true` when the value was NEW.

The return value saves a preceding `contains`, which would probe twice.

Members.Name: remove
Members.Signature: pub mut fn remove(value: T): bool
Members.Doc: Removes and returns `true` when the value was present.

Members.Name: clear
Members.Doc:
Empties the set. The backing arrays are KEPT, as in `List.clear`; the tombstones vanish
with everything else.

Members.Name: iter
Members.Doc: A fresh cursor on every call.

Items.Name: SetIterator
Items.Doc:
Walks the occupied slots. The order follows the hashes and is therefore UNSPECIFIED; a
caller that needs one sorts.

Members.Name: source
Members.Doc: The set being walked.

Members.Name: index
Members.Doc: The next slot to look at.

Members.Name: next
Members.Doc: The next value, or `null` at the end.

Items.Name: emptySet
Items.Doc: An empty set.

Items.Name: union
Items.Signature: pub fn union<T :: [Hashable<T>, Equatable<T>]>(a: Set<T>, b: Set<T>): Set<T>
Items.Doc: Everything in either set, as a NEW set; neither argument changes.

Items.Name: intersect
Items.Signature: pub fn intersect<T :: [Hashable<T>, Equatable<T>]>(a: Set<T>, b: Set<T>): Set<T>
Items.Doc: Everything in both sets, as a NEW set; neither argument changes.

Items.Name: difference
Items.Signature: pub fn difference<T :: [Hashable<T>, Equatable<T>]>(a: Set<T>, b: Set<T>): Set<T>
Items.Doc: Everything in `a` that is not in `b`, as a NEW set; neither argument changes.

Items.Name: isSubset
Items.Signature: pub fn isSubset<T :: [Hashable<T>, Equatable<T>]>(a: Set<T>, b: Set<T>): bool
Items.Doc: Whether every element of `a` is in `b`.

Items.Name: MapKeyIterator
Items.Doc: Walks the keys; the order follows the hashes and is UNSPECIFIED.

Members.Name: source
Members.Doc: The map being walked.

Members.Name: index
Members.Doc: The next slot to look at.

Members.Name: next
Members.Doc: The next key, or `null` at the end.

Items.Name: MapValueIterator
Items.Doc: Walks the values; the order follows the hashes and is UNSPECIFIED.

Members.Name: source
Members.Doc: The map being walked.

Members.Name: index
Members.Doc: The next slot to look at.

Members.Name: next
Members.Doc: The next value, or `null` at the end.

Items.Name: MapEntryIterator
Items.Signature: pub class MapEntryIterator<K :: [Hashable<K>, Equatable<K>], V> :: [Iterator<(K, V)>]
Items.Doc:
Walks key and value TOGETHER; the order follows the hashes and is UNSPECIFIED.

Without this, walking both meant iterating `keys` and paying a second probe per key
through `get`.

Members.Name: source
Members.Doc: The map being walked.

Members.Name: index
Members.Doc: The next slot to look at.

Members.Name: next
Members.Doc: The next `(key, value)` pair, or `null` at the end.

Items.Name: keys
Items.Signature: pub fn keys<K :: [Hashable<K>, Equatable<K>], V>(m: Map<K, V>): Iterator<K>
Items.Doc: A fresh cursor over the keys.

Items.Name: values
Items.Signature: pub fn values<K :: [Hashable<K>, Equatable<K>], V>(m: Map<K, V>): Iterator<V>
Items.Doc: A fresh cursor over the values.

Items.Name: entries
Items.Signature: pub fn entries<K :: [Hashable<K>, Equatable<K>], V>(m: Map<K, V>): Iterator<(K, V)>
Items.Doc:
A fresh cursor over `(key, value)` pairs:

    for (entry in entries(m)) { let (k, v) = entry; … }

Items.Name: listContains
Items.Signature: pub fn listContains<T :: [Equatable<T>]>(xs: List<T>, value: T): bool
Items.Doc: Whether the value occurs, by `equals`; O(n).

Items.Name: listIndexOf
Items.Signature: pub fn listIndexOf<T :: [Equatable<T>]>(xs: List<T>, value: T): ?int
Items.Doc: The position of the first occurrence, or `null` when there is none.

Modules.Doc:
What the language itself needs: aborting with a reason, the ready-made `Throwable`, and the
interfaces the built-in types satisfy.

`panic` and `coroutineEnded` are bound by the compiler, so nothing has to import this module to
reach them.

Items.Name: panic
Items.Doc:
Ends the program with `message` and a backtrace.

Not catchable. Its return type is `never`, so the flow analysis treats everything after a call as
unreachable — which is why `expect` can return a non-optional after panicking.

Items.Name: coroutineEnded
Items.Doc:
Panics because a coroutine was resumed after its body had run to the end.

Called from a dispatcher nobody wrote, which is why nobody could have written the import either.

Items.Name: assert
Items.Signature: pub fn assert(condition: bool, message: string): void
Items.Doc:
Panics with `message` when `condition` is false, for invariants the compiler does not check.

`void` rather than `never`: it does not replace a `return`, and a function ending in `assert` is
still `LYR-SEM0017`.

Items.Name: todo
Items.Doc:
Marks a place that is still missing. Unlike a comment it reports itself when reached, with
`not implemented:` before the message.

Items.Name: unreachable
Items.Doc:
Marks a branch that must never be taken, with `unreachable:` before the message.

`todo` means *still to come*; this means *must never happen*. Reaching it says that an assumption
stated somewhere else is wrong.

Items.Name: Exception
Items.Doc: The ready-made `Throwable` for throwing a message: `throw Exception { text = "…" };`.

Members.Name: text
Members.Doc: What `message()` returns.

Members.Name: message
Members.Doc: The text this exception was built with.

Items.Name: Display
Items.Doc:
What can be rendered as text — the anchor for `write`, `writeln` and `std.fmt`.

Every built-in scalar satisfies it through an `extend`, and a user type through `::`. A value
held THROUGH the interface (`let d: Display = 5;`) stays rejected: an interface value is a fat
pointer and needs a reference, which a scalar has none of.

Members.Name: show
Members.Doc: This value as text.

Items.Name: Equatable
Items.Doc:
Values of this type can be compared for equality.

Generic rather than `fn equals(other: Equatable)`, so both sides carry the concrete type: an
interface as a parameter type would need an interface VALUE, and a scalar cannot be one — there
would be no `Map<int, V>`.

Members.Name: equals
Members.Doc: Whether the two are equal.

Items.Name: Hashable
Items.Doc:
Values of this type can be hashed, which is what a `Map` key and a `Set` element need.

**Equal values must produce equal hashes.** No compiler checks it and every hash table depends on
it. The reverse does not hold — two different values may collide.

It does not imply `Equatable` yet — that adoption is a breaking change reserved for 2.0. A
caller needing both requires both: `K :: [Hashable<K>, Equatable<K>]`.

Members.Name: hash
Members.Doc: The hash of this value.

Items.Name: Ordered
Items.Doc:
Values of this type have an order — what sorting and range queries need.

One comparison instead of four methods: `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=` all derive from it.

Members.Name: compare
Members.Doc:
Negative when this comes first, zero when the two are equal, positive when `other` comes
first — as `strcmp`.

Items.Name: Add
Items.Doc: Values of this type can be added: `a + b` is `a.add(b)`.

Members.Name: add
Members.Doc: The sum of this value and `other`.

Items.Name: Sub
Items.Doc: Values of this type can be subtracted: `a - b` is `a.sub(b)`.

Members.Name: sub
Members.Doc: This value minus `other`.

Items.Name: Mul
Items.Doc: Values of this type can be multiplied: `a * b` is `a.mul(b)`.

Members.Name: mul
Members.Doc: The product of this value and `other`.

Items.Name: Div
Items.Doc: Values of this type can be divided: `a / b` is `a.div(b)`.

Members.Name: div
Members.Doc:
This value divided by `other`. What a division by zero does is the type's own business;
the built-in numerics panic.

Items.Name: Into
Items.Doc:
A value of this type converts to `T`: `x as T` is `x.into()`.

ONE target per type: the method is named `into`, and a type has one member of a name — a second
conversion is an ordinary named method. Total conversions only; a conversion that can fail
belongs in a named function returning an optional.

The numeric casts keep their opcodes: `1 as float` never goes through here.

Members.Name: into
Members.Doc: This value as a `T`.

Items.Name: OnModule
Items.Doc: A struct declaring this may stand as `@Name` before the module header.

Items.Name: OnType
Items.Doc: A struct declaring this may stand as `@Name` before a struct, class or enum declaration.

Items.Name: OnFunction
Items.Doc: A struct declaring this may stand as `@Name` before a top-level function.

Items.Name: Deprecated
Items.Doc:
Marks its target as deprecated: the compiler warns at every use, and `message` says what to
use instead. The first attribute the compiler itself reads — it changes diagnostics and
nothing else, so a program that ignores the warning runs unchanged.

Members.Name: message
Members.Doc: What to use instead; shown in the warning at every use site.

Items.Name: formatInt
Items.Signature: pub fn formatInt(value: int, spec: string): string
Items.Doc:
An `int` through a .NET numeric specifier (`N0`, `D5`, `X`, ...). An invalid specifier is a
panic rather than an error value: it is a literal in the source and does not depend on the
input.

Items.Name: formatUint
Items.Signature: pub fn formatUint(value: uint, spec: string): string
Items.Doc: A `uint` through a .NET numeric specifier; large values stay positive.

Items.Name: formatFloat
Items.Signature: pub fn formatFloat(value: float, spec: string): string
Items.Doc: A `float` through a .NET numeric specifier (`N2`, `F3`, `E2`, `P1`, ...).

Items.Name: formatBool
Items.Signature: pub fn formatBool(value: bool, spec: string): string
Items.Doc: A `bool` through a .NET specifier.

Items.Name: formatChar
Items.Signature: pub fn formatChar(value: char, spec: string): string
Items.Doc: A `char` through a .NET specifier.

Items.Name: formatString
Items.Signature: pub fn formatString(value: string, spec: string): string
Items.Doc:
A string at a width: padding on the right (`{name:10}`) or, with a leading minus, on the
left (`{name:-10}`).

Items.Name: formatRadix
Items.Signature: pub fn formatRadix(value: int, radix: int): string
Items.Doc:
To a base from 2 to 36. Letters from `a` for digit values above 9.

The inverse of `std.string.parseIntRadix`. They live in different modules because parsing is
text processing and formatting is output, and `std.string` must not import `std.fmt`.

Items.Name: formatHex
Items.Doc: Hexadecimal, lower case, no prefix.

Items.Name: formatBinary
Items.Doc: Binary, no prefix.

Items.Name: formatOctal
Items.Doc: Octal, no prefix.

Items.Name: formatHexPadded
Items.Signature: pub fn formatHexPadded(value: int, width: int): string
Items.Doc:
Hexadecimal with a fixed number of digits and leading zeros: `formatHexPadded(255, 4)` is
`"00ff"`, for addresses and colour values where the width carries meaning.

Items.Name: padLeft
Items.Signature: pub fn padLeft(value: string, width: int): string
Items.Doc: Pads with spaces at the FRONT until `width` is reached; longer strings stay unchanged.

Items.Name: padRight
Items.Signature: pub fn padRight(value: string, width: int): string
Items.Doc: Pads with spaces at the END until `width` is reached; longer strings stay unchanged.

Items.Name: center
Items.Signature: pub fn center(value: string, width: int): string
Items.Doc:
Centres. On an odd remainder the extra character goes to the RIGHT.
A decision rather than a matter of course, but without it the same input yields two different
results depending on the implementation.

Items.Name: formatBytes
Items.Doc:
Bytes in readable form: `1536` becomes `"1.5 KB"`.

Base 1024 with the prefixes without `i` (`KB` rather than `KiB`), the spelling operating
systems and tools actually use.

Items.Name: table
Items.Signature: pub fn table(rows: string[][], separator: string): string
Items.Doc:
Aligns columns. Each row is a `string[]`; short rows are padded with empty cells.

No borders and no header handling: what a table means is the caller's business. This does the
tedious part — two passes over the data, to know the column widths before printing.

Modules.Doc:
Reading from and writing to the console.

Output needs no capability — it is always available. `print` and `println` take any type that
satisfies `Display`: `println(42)`, `println(true)`, `println("hi")`.

Items.Name: print
Items.Doc:
Writes any displayable value without a line break: `print(42)`, `print("hi")`.

There is no overloading; the `Display` constraint does the same job and extends to every type
that satisfies it rather than to a fixed list. Monomorphization turns the call into a direct one
per used type, so the generality costs nothing at runtime.

Nothing is flushed. A prompt written with `print` sits in the buffer until `flush`, which is why
`prompt` exists.

Items.Name: println
Items.Doc: Writes any displayable value, followed by a line break.

Items.Name: eprint
Items.Doc: Writes any displayable value to standard ERROR without a line break.

Items.Name: eprintln
Items.Doc:
Writes any displayable value to standard ERROR, followed by a line break.

Diagnostics belong here rather than in standard output, so a program used in a pipe does not put
them into the data.

Items.Name: write
Items.Doc: Writes any displayable value without a line break.

Items.Name: writeln
Items.Doc: Writes any displayable value, followed by a line break.

Items.Name: readLine
Items.Doc:
Reads one line from standard input, without its line break.

`null` at end of input. Optional rather than an empty string, because EOF is a state and not a
line: a program reading until `null` stops, one reading until `""` never does.

Items.Name: readAll
Items.Doc:
Reads everything up to end of input, for filters that need the whole text.

The input is held in memory in full. `lines` is the way through a stream larger than that.

Items.Name: readChar
Items.Doc: Reads a single code point, or `null` at end of input.

Items.Name: isInteractive
Items.Doc:
Whether standard input and output are a terminal rather than a pipe.

A program writing into a pipe should not put a prompt into the stream, and this is how it knows.

Items.Name: flush
Items.Doc:
Pushes buffered output to the console.

Needed as soon as something is written without a line break and has to be visible before the
program continues — a prompt being the usual case.

Items.Name: prompt
Items.Doc:
Writes `text`, flushes it, and reads one line.

The flush is the point: without it the question would sit in the buffer while the program waits
for an answer nobody knows is expected. `null` at end of input, as `readLine`.

Items.Name: LineIterator
Items.Doc: The iterator `lines` hands out. Yields each line of standard input until it ends.

Members.Name: done
Members.Doc: Set once `readLine` answered `null`; from then on the iterator ends.

Members.Name: next
Members.Doc: The next line, or `null` once the input has ended. Ends for good after the first `null`.

Items.Name: lines
Items.Doc:
The lines of standard input, as an iterator — the idiomatic shape of a filter:

    for (line in console.lines()) { … }

An iterator rather than a `string[]`: the input can be larger than memory, and a program that
only counts should not have to collect it first.

Items.Name: readText
Items.Doc:
The whole content as text, decoded as UTF-8 — bytes that are not valid UTF-8 become
U+FFFD. For binary data use `readBytes`. `null` when the file does not exist or is not
readable.

Items.Name: writeText
Items.Signature: pub fn writeText(path: string, content: string): bool
Items.Doc: Writes text (UTF-8), replacing an existing file. `true` on success.

Items.Name: appendText
Items.Signature: pub fn appendText(path: string, content: string): bool
Items.Doc: Appends to an existing file or creates it. `true` on success.

Items.Name: exists
Items.Doc: Whether something — file or directory — exists at the path.

Items.Name: remove
Items.Doc: `true` when the file is gone afterwards, including when it never existed.

Items.Name: readBytes
Items.Doc:
The raw bytes, undecoded — what `readText` cannot give: its UTF-8 decoding turns invalid
bytes into U+FFFD. An unreadable file reads as empty, the `readLines` convention; a caller
that needs the difference asks `exists` first.

Items.Name: writeBytes
Items.Signature: pub fn writeBytes(path: string, data: uint8[]): bool
Items.Doc:
Writes raw bytes, replacing an existing file. `true` on success — the `writeText`
convention. (v1.14: the first native whose parameter is an array.)

Items.Name: appendBytes
Items.Signature: pub fn appendBytes(path: string, data: uint8[]): bool
Items.Doc: Appends raw bytes to an existing file or creates it. `true` on success.

Items.Name: readLines
Items.Doc:
The lines of a file, or an empty array when it is not readable. Terminators are removed,
so whether the file used CRLF or LF is no longer visible.

Items.Name: size
Items.Doc: The size in bytes, or `null` when the file does not exist.

Items.Name: isFile
Items.Doc: Whether the path names an existing FILE.

Items.Name: isDirectory
Items.Doc: Whether the path names an existing DIRECTORY.

Items.Name: copy
Items.Signature: pub fn copy(from: string, to: string): bool
Items.Doc: Copies. `false` when the source is missing or the target is not writable.

Items.Name: move
Items.Signature: pub fn move(from: string, to: string): bool
Items.Doc: Moves or renames; the same operation on every file system.

Items.Name: createDir
Items.Doc: Creates one directory; the parent must exist. `createDirAll` creates the chain.

Items.Name: createDirAll
Items.Doc: Creates missing parent directories too. An existing directory counts as success.

Items.Name: removeDir
Items.Doc:
Deletes an EMPTY directory. There is no recursive delete; a caller that needs one writes
the loop visibly.

Items.Name: listDir
Items.Doc:
The entries of a directory: names rather than paths, sorted alphabetically.

An empty array for an unreadable directory rather than a `?string[]`, as in `readLines`. A
caller that needs the difference asks `isDirectory` first.

Items.Name: tempDir
Items.Doc: A path in the system's temporary directory. Does NOT create the file.

Items.Name: joinPath
Items.Signature: pub fn joinPath(left: string, right: string): string
Items.Doc: Joins two path parts, with neither a doubled nor a missing separator.

Items.Name: fileName
Items.Doc: The last component. `"a/b/c.txt"` becomes `"c.txt"`.

Items.Name: parentDir
Items.Doc: Everything before the last separator, or `""` when there is none.

Items.Name: extension
Items.Doc:
The extension WITHOUT the dot. `""` when there is none.

A leading dot does not count: `".gitignore"` has no extension, that is its name. This rule
differs between languages, so it is stated here.

Items.Name: stem
Items.Doc: The name without its extension. `"a/b/c.txt"` becomes `"c"`.

Items.Name: withExtension
Items.Signature: pub fn withExtension(path: string, ext: string): string
Items.Doc: Replaces the extension. An empty extension removes it.

A container SAYS how to walk it rather than being the cursor itself — were `List<T>` its own
`Iterator<T>`, two loops over the same list would push each other along. Every call hands out
a FRESH cursor.

exist separately because `fold` with a closure is too much ceremony for counting.

Modules.Doc:
Computing with `?T` without testing first.

There is no `Option<T>` here — `?T` is it, and these are functions over the built-in type.
Absent on purpose, because the language already has them: `unwrap` is `o!`, `unwrapOr` is
`o ?? fallback`, and `isSome`/`isNone` are `o != null`/`o == null`, which is what flow narrowing
keys on. A function would cut that off: after `if (isSome(o))`, `o` would still be a `?T`.

Items.Name: map
Items.Signature: pub fn map<T, U>(o: ?T, f: fn(T) -> U): ?U
Items.Doc: Applies `f` to the value when there is one, and answers `null` when there is not.

Items.Name: andThen
Items.Signature: pub fn andThen<T, U>(o: ?T, f: fn(T) -> ?U): ?U
Items.Doc:
As `map`, but `f` may itself come back empty.

This takes the place of `flatten`: a `map` whose `f` returned `?U` would produce a `??U`, which
is not a type. Here `f` already returns `?U` and the result is that same `?U`.

Items.Doc: Keeps the value only when `pred` accepts it, and answers `null` otherwise.

Items.Name: zip
Items.Signature: pub fn zip<T, U>(a: ?T, b: ?U): ?(T, U)
Items.Doc:
Both present yields a tuple, otherwise `null`.

The result is taken apart with `let (a, b) = …`.

Items.Signature: pub fn lastIndexOf(value: string, needle: string): int
Items.Doc: The LAST occurrence.

Items.Name: count
Items.Signature: pub fn count(value: string, needle: string): int
Items.Doc:
How often `needle` occurs, WITHOUT overlap.

Overlapping occurrences are not counted: `count("aaa", "aa")` is 1, not 2. This matches
`replace`.

Items.Name: join
Items.Signature: pub fn join(parts: string[], separator: string): string
Items.Doc:
Joins the parts with a separator: the inverse of `split`. One native call — a left fold
would copy the whole result once per part.

Items.Name: splitLines
Items.Doc: Splits at line breaks. Both `\r\n` and `\n` count.

Items.Name: splitFirst
Items.Signature: pub fn splitFirst(value: string, separator: string): string[]
Items.Doc: Splits at the FIRST occurrence; the rest stays whole, for `key=value=more`.

Items.Name: replace
Items.Signature: pub fn replace(value: string, needle: string, replacement: string): string
Items.Doc: Every non-overlapping occurrence of `needle` replaced. An empty needle changes nothing.

Items.Name: replaceFirst
Items.Signature: pub fn replaceFirst(value: string, needle: string, replacement: string): string
Items.Doc: The first occurrence replaced; without one the string comes back unchanged.

Items.Name: trimStart
Items.Doc: Without leading whitespace.

Items.Name: trimEnd
Items.Doc: Without trailing whitespace.

Items.Name: padStart
Items.Signature: pub fn padStart(value: string, width: int, fill: char): string
Items.Doc:
Pads at the front until `width` is reached. A longer string is left unchanged; truncating
would lose data in a function that only formats.

Items.Name: padEnd
Items.Signature: pub fn padEnd(value: string, width: int, fill: char): string
Items.Doc:
Pads at the end until `width` is reached. A longer string is left unchanged; truncating
would lose data in a function that only formats.

Items.Name: parseInt
Items.Doc:
`"-42"` becomes `-42`, anything else `null`.

No overflow protection: a number beyond `int64` wraps rather than yielding `null`. Detecting
it would need a division per digit.

Items.Name: parseIntRadix
Items.Signature: pub fn parseIntRadix(value: string, radix: int): ?int
Items.Doc: From a base of 2 to 36. Letters continue from `a`/`A`.

Items.Name: parseBool
Items.Doc: Exactly `"true"` or `"false"`; anything else is `null`.

Items.Name: parseFloat
Items.Doc:
`"3.5"`, `"-0.25"` and `"42"` become floating point; everything else is `null`.

Without exponent notation (`1e9`), which would need a state machine of its own.

Items.Name: StringBuilder
Items.Doc:
Builds a string piece by piece.

`s = s + part` in a loop is quadratic: every step copies the whole string so far. The builder
collects the parts and joins them once.

The backing is a doubling `string[]`, written by hand because this module must not import
`std.collections`.

Members.Name: parts
Members.Doc: The collected pieces; `count` says how many are filled.

Members.Name: count
Members.Doc: How many entries of `parts` are real.

Members.Name: new
Members.Doc: An empty builder.

Members.Name: length
Members.Doc:
How many pieces were appended — the PIECE count, an implementation detail, NOT the
character count. Measure the built string instead. (It would carry `@Deprecated`, but an
attribute cannot sit on a member yet; the removal is planned for 2.0 regardless.)

Members.Name: append
Members.Signature: pub mut fn append(value: string): void
Members.Doc: Adds a piece; the backing array doubles when full.

Members.Name: appendLine
Members.Signature: pub mut fn appendLine(value: string): void
Members.Doc: Adds the piece and a `\n`.

Members.Name: appendChar
Members.Signature: pub mut fn appendChar(value: char): void
Members.Doc: Adds one character.

Members.Name: build
Members.Doc:
The pieces joined once — the point of collecting them. One native call over the filled
slice; a left fold would copy the whole result once per piece, the exact cost the
builder exists to avoid. Reads and never consumes: building twice yields the same
string.

Items.Name: newStringBuilder
Items.Doc: An empty builder.

Modules.Doc:
Marking tests, and the assertions that fail them. `lyric test` runs every function marked
`@Test` in the project's test root; a test fails by panicking, which is what the assertions
here do.

Items.Name: Test
Items.Doc:
Marks a top-level function as a test. `lyric test` finds it through the attribute row and
runs it in a fresh instance; the function takes no parameters and returns nothing.

Items.Name: assertTrue
Items.Signature: pub fn assertTrue(condition: bool, message: string): void
Items.Doc:
Fails the test with `message` when `condition` is false.

The same behavior as `std.core.assert` — it exists so a test file needs one import, and it
delegates so there is one implementation.

Items.Name: assertEq
Items.Signature: pub fn assertEq<T :: [Equatable<T>, Display]>(actual: T, expected: T): void
Items.Doc: Fails the test when the two values differ, naming both.

Items.Name: Duration
Items.Doc:
A distance between two instants, in whole milliseconds. May be negative: `a.since(b)` with
`b` later than `a` says so rather than hiding it.

Members.Name: millis
Members.Doc: The distance in milliseconds; the sign is the direction.

Members.Name: ofMillis
Members.Signature: pub static fn ofMillis(value: int): Duration
Members.Doc: A duration of whole milliseconds.

Members.Name: ofSeconds
Members.Signature: pub static fn ofSeconds(value: int): Duration
Members.Doc: A duration of whole seconds.

Members.Name: ofMinutes
Members.Signature: pub static fn ofMinutes(value: int): Duration
Members.Doc: A duration of whole minutes.

Members.Name: totalMillis
Members.Doc: The whole distance in milliseconds.

Members.Name: totalSeconds
Members.Doc: The whole distance in seconds, truncated towards zero.

Members.Name: plus
Members.Doc: The two added.

Members.Name: minus
Members.Doc: The other subtracted from this one.

Items.Name: Instant
Items.Doc: A point on the wall clock: milliseconds since 1970-01-01 UTC.

Members.Name: millis
Members.Doc: Milliseconds since the epoch; negative is before 1970.

Members.Name: now
Members.Doc: The wall clock, now.

Members.Name: ofEpochMillis
Members.Signature: pub static fn ofEpochMillis(value: int): Instant
Members.Doc:
The instant at these epoch milliseconds — for stored timestamps and for tests, which
want a clock that stands still.

Members.Name: epochMillis
Members.Doc: Milliseconds since the epoch — the raw number back, for storing.

Members.Name: since
Members.Doc: The distance from `earlier` to this instant. Negative when `earlier` is actually later.

Members.Name: plus
Members.Doc: This instant moved by a duration; a negative one moves backwards.

Members.Name: iso
Members.Doc:
ISO 8601 in UTC, millisecond precision: `1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z`.

`divFloor`/`modFloor` rather than `/` and `%`, so an instant BEFORE the epoch lands in
the right day — truncation would round the day towards 1970 and hand the rest a negative
time.
